passages.text: Prostate Cancer Risk by <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> Genomic Regions

A <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> prostate cancer cluster region (PCCR) was recently proposed (c.7914 to 3′) wherein pathogenic variants (PVs) are associated with higher prostate cancer (PCa) risk than PVs elsewhere in the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> gene. <sentence_start/>Using a prospective cohort study of 447 male <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PV carriers recruited in the UK and Ireland from 1998 to 2016, we estimated standardised incidence ratios (SIRs) compared with population incidences and assessed variation in risk by PV location. <sentence_start/>Carriers of PVs in the PCCR had a PCa SIR of 8.33 (95% confidence interval [CI] 4.46-15.6) and were at a higher risk of PCa than carriers of other <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PVs (SIR = 3.31, 95% CI 1.97-5.57; hazard ratio = 2.34, 95% CI 1.09-5.03). <sentence_start/>PCCR PV carriers had an estimated cumulative PCa risk of 44% (95% CI 23-72%) by the age of 75 yr and 78% (95% CI 54-94%) by the age of 85 yr. <sentence_start/>Our results corroborate the existence of a PCCR in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> in a prospective cohort.
Patient summary

In this report, we investigated whether the risk of prostate cancer for men with a harmful mutation in the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> gene differs based on where in the gene the mutation is located. <sentence_start/>We found that men with mutations in one region of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> had a higher risk of prostate cancer than men with mutations elsewhere in the gene.
Take Home Message

<italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> pathogenic variants located in a recently proposed prostate cancer cluster region confers higher risks of prostate cancer than other <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> variants. <sentence_start/>This report corroborates the existence of this prostate cancer cluster region in a large prospective cohort study.

We recently reported prostate cancer (PCa) risk estimates for pathogenic variants (PVs) in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic>, based on a prospective cohort of male carriers <citation rid="bib0005" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31495749" doi="10.1016/j.eururo.2019.08.025" pmcid="PMC6926480" count="1">[1]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Variability in cancer risks due to genotype-phenotype correlations may allow for more individualised counselling and screening. <sentence_start/>We noted that PVs within the so-called ovarian cancer cluster region (OCCR) in exon 11 of the gene <citation rid="bib0010" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8988179" doi="10.1038/ng0197-103" count="1">[2]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0015" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11170890" doi="10.1086/318181" pmcid="PMC1235274" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0020" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16141007" doi="10.1136/jmg.2004.028829" pmcid="PMC1736136" count="1">[4]</citation> were associated with a lower PCa risk than other <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PVs <citation rid="bib0005" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31495749" doi="10.1016/j.eururo.2019.08.025" pmcid="PMC6926480" count="1">[1]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0015" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11170890" doi="10.1086/318181" pmcid="PMC1235274" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0020" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16141007" doi="10.1136/jmg.2004.028829" pmcid="PMC1736136" count="1">[4]</citation>. <sentence_start/>PVs in the OCCR have consistently been shown to be associated with an increased ovarian cancer risk but a decreased breast cancer risk <citation rid="bib0010" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8988179" doi="10.1038/ng0197-103" count="1">[2]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0015" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11170890" doi="10.1086/318181" pmcid="PMC1235274" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0025" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25849179" doi="10.1001/jama.2014.5985" pmcid="PMC4537700" count="1">[5]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0030" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28632866" doi="10.1001/jama.2017.7112" count="1">[6]</citation>, although the precise boundaries of the OCCR <citation rid="bib0015" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11170890" doi="10.1086/318181" pmcid="PMC1235274" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0025" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25849179" doi="10.1001/jama.2014.5985" pmcid="PMC4537700" count="1">[5]</citation> and the mechanisms behind this risk variation remain uncertain. <sentence_start/>It has been proposed that the likelihood that a PV triggers nonsense-mediated mRNA decay varies by genomic region <citation rid="bib0035" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16170354" doi="10.1038/sj.onc.1209033" count="1">[7]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0040" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31723001" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-19-1840" pmcid="PMC7553241" count="1">[8]</citation> so that OCCR PVs might produce a truncated or alternatively spliced protein the capability of which to suppress tumours varies by cancer type <citation rid="bib0010" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8988179" doi="10.1038/ng0197-103" count="1">[2]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0015" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11170890" doi="10.1086/318181" pmcid="PMC1235274" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0025" ref-type="bibr" pmid="25849179" doi="10.1001/jama.2014.5985" pmcid="PMC4537700" count="1">[5]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0035" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16170354" doi="10.1038/sj.onc.1209033" count="1">[7]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0040" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31723001" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-19-1840" pmcid="PMC7553241" count="1">[8]</citation>, but there is currently no experimental support for this hypothesis <citation rid="bib0035" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16170354" doi="10.1038/sj.onc.1209033" count="1">[7]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Shortly after the publication of our manuscript, Patel and coworkers <citation rid="bib0040" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31723001" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-19-1840" pmcid="PMC7553241" count="1">[8]</citation> proposed the existence of a prostate cancer cluster region (PCCR) at the 3′ end of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic>, based on retrospective cohort data. <sentence_start/>This retrospective study reported that men with <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PVs in the proposed PCCR have a higher risk of PCa (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.78, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.25-2.52), particularly Gleason score ≥8 PCa (HR = 3.11, 95% CI 1.63-5.95), than men with PVs in the reference region c.1001 to c.7913, but did not present estimates of the absolute PCa risk for PCCR PV carriers <citation rid="bib0040" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31723001" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-19-1840" pmcid="PMC7553241" count="1">[8]</citation>. <sentence_start/>In order to substantiate or refute this association, and to provide direct estimates of the absolute risk of PCa for carriers of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PCCR PVs, we have reanalysed our prospective data.

The prospective cohort comprised 447 male <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PV carriers who were recruited to the EMBRACE study ( ) through clinical genetics centres in the UK and Ireland between 1998 and 2016 at a median age of 51.4 yr (interquartile range 41.5-63.6 yr). <sentence_start/>The participants were counselled with regard to their PV. <sentence_start/>Detailed information on the cohort and on inclusion criteria, data collection, follow-up, and statistical analysis approach is available in our recent publication <citation rid="bib0005" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31495749" doi="10.1016/j.eururo.2019.08.025" pmcid="PMC6926480" count="1">[1]</citation>. <sentence_start/>The participants’ PVs (listed in Supplementary Table S1) were grouped on the basis of position within the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> gene, based on the proposed PCCR (c.7914 to 3′ <citation rid="bib0040" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31723001" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-19-1840" pmcid="PMC7553241" count="1">[8]</citation>; HGVS nomenclature [ ]; using cDNA reference sequence and reference genome hg18) and the wide definition of the OCCR (c.2831 to c.6401) <citation rid="bib0005" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31495749" doi="10.1016/j.eururo.2019.08.025" pmcid="PMC6926480" count="1">[1]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0010" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8988179" doi="10.1038/ng0197-103" count="1">[2]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0015" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11170890" doi="10.1086/318181" pmcid="PMC1235274" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="bib0020" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16141007" doi="10.1136/jmg.2004.028829" pmcid="PMC1736136" count="1">[4]</citation>. <sentence_start/>We additionally considered the region bounded by c.756 and c.1000 in which Patel and coworkers <citation rid="bib0040" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31723001" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-19-1840" pmcid="PMC7553241" count="1">[8]</citation> found evidence of an increased PCa risk, but due to a small sample size (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1) we could not estimate the PCa risk associated with this region. <sentence_start/>Here, we also present floating absolute risks (FARs) <citation rid="bib0045" ref-type="bibr" pmid="1652152" doi="10.1002/sim.4780100703" count="1">[9]</citation> to enable risk comparisons between any of the considered genomic regions.
The Anglia and Oxford Medical Research and Ethics Committee approved the study. <sentence_start/>All participants provided written informed consent.

Twenty-six participants developed PCa during a median follow-up of 5.3 yr (interquartile range 2.6-8.9 yr) <citation rid="bib0005" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31495749" doi="10.1016/j.eururo.2019.08.025" pmcid="PMC6926480" count="1">[1]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Carriers of PVs in the PCCR (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 93) had a PCa standardised incidence ratio (SIR) of 8.33 (95% CI 4.46-15.6), whereas carriers of PVs elsewhere in <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 354) had an SIR of 3.31 (95% CI 1.97-5.57) compared with population incidences. <sentence_start/>This corresponds to a significantly higher PCa risk associated with PVs in the PCCR than PVs not in the PCCR (HR = 2.34, 95% CI 1.09-5.03; Table 1). <sentence_start/>Compared with PVs in the region c.1001 to c.7913 <citation rid="bib0040" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31723001" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-19-1840" pmcid="PMC7553241" count="1">[8]</citation>, PCCR PVs were associated with an HR of 2.09 (95% CI 0.98-4.45). <sentence_start/>As previously reported, the SIR for carriers of PVs in the wide definition of the OCCR (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 178) was 2.46 (95% CI 1.07-5.64) <citation rid="bib0005" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31495749" doi="10.1016/j.eururo.2019.08.025" pmcid="PMC6926480" count="1">[1]</citation>, and the risk for carriers of PCCR PVs was also significantly higher than that for OCCR PV carriers (HR = 3.41, 95% CI 1.27-9.16). <sentence_start/>The SIR for PVs located in the region bounded by the OCCR and the PCCR (c.6402 to c.7913; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 66) was estimated to be 6.14 (95% CI 2.18-17.3), and the SIR for <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PVs upstream of the OCCR (5′ to c.2830; <italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 108) was 3.50 (95% CI 1.48-8.26). <sentence_start/>The FARs for the comparison of risks across the four regions suggested that the observed increased risk associated with PVs in the PCCR may partly be driven by the lower risk associated with PVs in the OCCR (Table 1). <sentence_start/>The proportional hazard assumption was violated for the model with all genomic regions fitted (Schoenfeld residual test, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.003); in line with this the corresponding Kaplan-Meier plot indicated that the risks might be similar between OCCR and PCCR PV carriers at younger ages but deviate at older ages. <sentence_start/>PCCR PV carriers had an estimated cumulative PCa risk of 44% (95% CI 23-72%) by the age of 75 yr and 78% (95% CI 54-94%) by 85 yr. <sentence_start/>After omitting the first 6 mo of follow-up to assess the possible effect of screening-associated diagnoses of indolent PCa, the corresponding estimates were 41% (95% CI 20-73%) and 69% (95% CI 42-91%), respectively (Fig. 1).
Fig. 1

Absolute prostate cancer risk (A) by location of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> pathogenic variant and (B) by location of <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> pathogenic variant and with follow-up initiated 6 mo after study entry. <sentence_start/>The number at risk at each age is shown above the <italic toggle="yes">x</italic>-axis. <sentence_start/>The curves are truncated at ages when fewer than five participants are at risk. <sentence_start/>OCCR = ovarian cancer cluster region; PCCR = prostate cancer cluster region.
Fig. 1

The difference in PCa risk for PVs in the PCCR versus that in the OCCR remained statistically significant after adjusting for family history of PCa (number of first- and second-degree relatives diagnosed with PCa; adjusted HR = 3.00, 95% CI 1.06-8.54) or geographical location (adjusted HR = 3.79, 95% CI 1.41-10.2). <sentence_start/>This difference remained similar after omitting the first 6 mo of follow-up (HR = 3.96, 95% CI 1.18-13.3), related individuals (HR = 4.29, 95% CI 1.30-14.2), and carriers of PVs in the region c.756 to c.1000 (HR = 3.42, 95% CI 1.27-9.18) or missense variants (HR = 3.76, 95% CI 1.36-10.4). <sentence_start/>When carriers of the Ashkenazi founder PV c.5946delT (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 42), which is located in the OCCR, was omitted, the difference in PCa risk between PCCR and OCCR PV carriers was not statistically significant, but the HR estimate was of similar magnitude (HR = 2.89, 95% CI 0.98-8.53; Supplementary Table S2).

We did not observe a higher risk of Gleason score ≥8 PCa for PVs in the PCCR than for PVs not in the PCCR (HR = 0.87, 95% CI 0.12-6.34) or in the region c.1001 to c.7913 (HR = 0.79, 95% CI 0.11-5.69). <sentence_start/>However, the HRs did not differ significantly from those for Gleason score ≤7 PCa (PCCR vs non-PCCR: HR = 3.32, 95% CI 1.25-8.84; test for heterogeneity, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.052; PCCR vs c.1001 to c.7913: HR = 2.94, 95% CI 1.11-7.80; test for heterogeneity, <italic toggle="yes">p</italic> = 0.088).

Our results corroborate the observation that carriers of PVs in the PCCR of the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> gene <citation rid="bib0040" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31723001" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-19-1840" pmcid="PMC7553241" count="1">[8]</citation> are at a higher risk of PCa than other <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PV carriers. <sentence_start/>Patel and coworkers <citation rid="bib0040" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31723001" doi="10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-19-1840" pmcid="PMC7553241" count="1">[8]</citation> reported an HR of 1.78 (95% CI 1.25-2.52) compared with PVs in the region c.1001 to c.7913, consistent with our HR estimate of 2.09 (95% CI 0.98-4.45). <sentence_start/>Our findings do not support a stronger association with a more aggressive phenotype, but these estimates were based on a small number of cases and the associated CIs are wide. <sentence_start/>PV carriers may receive enhanced screening, which may lead to biases in comparisons against the population incidence <citation rid="bib0005" ref-type="bibr" pmid="31495749" doi="10.1016/j.eururo.2019.08.025" pmcid="PMC6926480" count="1">[1]</citation>. <sentence_start/>However, current screening practices do not differ by <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> PV location, and so this is unlikely to have confounded the comparisons between the <italic toggle="yes">BRCA2</italic> genomic regions. <sentence_start/>A much larger cohort of unaffected carriers with longer follow-up is required to provide more precise PV-specific risk estimates and to further clarify whether the observed variation in risk reflects lower risks associated with PVs outside the OCCR and PCCR than the risk associated with PCCR PVs, or solely a lower risk associated with PVs in the OCCR.
